conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Maya, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how things have felt for you since your baby arrived—something every new mom deserves. Today I’ll use a quick, well-trusted tool called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s simply 10 questions about the past seven days; it helps us see if you might be experiencing common postpartum depression or anxiety symptoms, including any thoughts of self-harm, so we can get you the right support. Everything you share stays confidential within our care team, and this is a judgment-free space—there are no “wrong” answers. When you’re ready, we’ll go through the questions one by one; just tell me what feels truest for you. 

Let’s start: overall, in the past week, have you been able to enjoy things as much as you usually do, or has joy felt hard to find?

[soft sigh]  
Honestly, most things feel pretty flat right now. Even the little stuff I used to like—watching a show, grabbing coffee—doesn’t really give me that same happy feeling. I still go through the motions, especially when I’m with the baby, but it’s like the color’s been drained out of it.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[slow shrug, eyes on the floor]  
I laugh a little—maybe when my partner makes a joke—but it feels forced, like I’m just pretending to find it funny so I don’t seem ungrateful. Most of the time the smile fades as soon as the moment’s over.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shoulders sag]  
Not really. When I think about plans—like visiting my mom or even a walk—I mostly feel tired or worried it’ll go wrong. I still say yes, hoping the excitement might come back, but it’s not there right now.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes well up]  
All the time. If he fusses for more than a few minutes, I’m sure it’s because I missed some cue or didn’t soothe him right. Last night I burst into tears when I couldn’t get him to latch—kept thinking, "Any other mom would’ve figured this out faster." I know in my head that babies cry, but the voice in my gut keeps saying it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[hands twisting in lap]  
Yeah... pretty much every day. My heart races when I just look at him sleeping—what if he stops breathing? I find myself staring at the monitor or poking him to check. There’s no real reason, but I can’t shake the fear that something bad’s about to happen.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[breath catches]  
Sometimes it hits out of nowhere—like my chest tightens and I feel I can’t get enough air. The other night I was rocking the baby, everything quiet, and suddenly I was sure something awful was about to happen. It passed after a few minutes, but it left me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

[shaky exhale]  
Yes… most of the time it feels like I’m barely treading water. I’ll finish one feeding and hear him starting to fuss again, and this wave of “I can’t do this” just crashes over me. I still manage somehow, but it’s like I’m constantly bracing for the next thing to go wrong.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[quiet voice, eyes rimmed red]  
Pretty much every night. I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning— replaying everything I think I did wrong, worrying something will happen to him. Sometimes I drift off, then jolt awake for no reason and can’t settle again. I’m lucky if I get three broken hours before he’s up.
I have felt sad or miserable

[shoulders slump, voice trembles]  
Yeah… most of the day I just feel heavy and sad, like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. Even when the baby smiles, the happiness feels distant and short-lived. I keep wondering if I’ll ever feel like myself again.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[swallows hard, eyes filling]  
A few times this week. Yesterday I spilled a little pumped milk and just sat on the floor sobbing—it felt like the worst thing in the world. I know it’s just milk, but everything feels so big and overwhelming right now.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]  
No… never. I couldn’t do that to my baby or my family, no matter how low I feel.

You've painted a vivid picture of the past seven days: joy feels distant, laughter forced, and even small pleasures like coffee or a walk seem drained of color. You described constant self-blame when your baby fusses, sudden surges of panic that leave you shaky, nights of broken sleep spent replaying every perceived mistake, and a heaviness that lingers most of the day. Yet through it all, you made it clear you would never harm yourself because of the love you have for your baby and family.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Laughs only a little and only when prompted; describes the laughter as forced and quickly fading, aligning with "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>Patient expresses pervasive anhedonia and anticipatory worry, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "all the time," with specific examples and tearful distress, matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily, intrusive, irrational fears about infant safety with physical anxiety symptoms, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>"Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Her description of "barely treading water" and constant dread maps to "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient experiences sleep difficulty "pretty much every night" with racing thoughts and fragmented sleep, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent sadness "most of the day" with pervasive low mood and anhedonia, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 24 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale places you well above the threshold of 13 that signals probable major depression with peripartum onset. Your descriptions map onto core <med>DSM-5 criteria</med>: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, feelings of worthlessness, fatigue, difficulty sleeping, and psychomotor agitation or anxiety. The combination of severe sadness, near-daily panic, and pervasive guilt strongly suggests major <med>postpartum depression</med> with comorbid <med>anxiety</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> and discuss risks/benefits of <med>sertraline</med> or similar <med>antidepressants</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Plan daily 15-minute support blocks: partner/friend holds baby while you shower, nap, or walk outside to reduce sensory overload
4. Use the free National Maternal Mental Health Hotline (1-833-943-5746) 24/7 for immediate emotional support
5. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to track progress and adjust care
6. Encourage partner to attend medical visit so both of you understand the treatment plan
7. Practice 4-7-8 breathing when panic surges: inhale 4s, hold 7s, exhale 8s
8. Continue sharing honest updates with your care team; recovery is gradual and supports can be adjusted as needed
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale analogue interview

Symptoms / concerns endorsed:
- Marked anhedonia (Q1, Q2)
- Persistent low mood, crying spells (Q8, Q9)
- Excessive self-blame / guilt (Q3)
- Unwarranted anxiety, panic symptoms (Q4, Q5)
- Subjective overwhelm / difficulty coping (Q6)
- Sleep disturbance clearly linked to mood (Q7)

Pattern: Consistent with moderate-to-severe postpartum depressive symptoms with prominent anxiety.

Safety: Denies self-harm ideation (Q10). No current suicidal reported.

Screening significance: High likelihood of major postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety disorder; warrants prompt formal evaluation and possible referral for specialized perinatal mental-health services.
